headline: The Race Holds at 69.4°F: Bass Working the Ledges While Bonito Build to the East
subhead: A five-degree spread between Kings Point and New London is steering the bite, and the current break at Valiant Rock is still the sharpest tool in the box.
body_markdown:
Sixty-nine point four degrees at New London this week, five and a half degrees cooler than the 70.9 reading out at Kings Point. That gradient is the whole story for the eastern Sound right now. The western basin is running warm and soft, the kind of water that pushes stripers off the flats and into structure by mid-morning. Out here at The Race, Plum Gut, and the Sluiceway, the faster water and deeper thermal layer are keeping fish more honest through the day, even if the bite itself has settled into what late August usually gives us — a real but grinding pattern, not a blitz.

This is the summer holding pattern, plain and simple. We said it a few days back and it's holding true: the true fall push doesn't start until nighttime temps start dropping hard, likely mid-September. Until then, the bass in this zone are working the classic late-summer program — deep structure by day, current edges at first and last light, and a stronger night bite than most weekend anglers ever fish. Race Rock and the ledge running west off Valiant Rock remain the most consistent stretch. That bottom rises out of over a hundred feet of moving water to inside thirty on the shoal itself, and on a hard ebb the seam it throws is still the best current break in the region. Wire line trolled with bunker spoons and umbrella rigs is producing fish in the twenty-to-thirty-four inch range along that edge, with a scattering of better fish pushing forty holding tighter to the rock on the last two hours of the ebb, right before slack.

Bucktail guys working the drift with six and eight-ounce heads dressed in white or chartreuse tube are doing better tucking bottom bounces into the deeper pocket on the east side of Valiant, letting the jig ride the current down into the eddy rather than fighting straight against it. That eddy is where the bait's been stacking — mostly peanut bunker and juvenile menhaden pushed in tight by the faster water outside. Slack itself is short here, fifteen to twenty minutes at best on a strong moon tide, so anyone working wire or heavy jigs needs to be ready the moment the rip starts to soften, not after it's already running the other way.

Bluefish remain the one constant nobody's complaining about. Cocktail blues in the three-to-six-pound range are mixing right into the bass catch on the same wire spreads and bucktails, and snapper-sized fish are thick enough in the back coves off Fishers Island and around Plum Gut's inner edges to keep any kid with a bobber and spearing busy for an afternoon. If the striper bite goes quiet on a given tide, there's almost always blues willing to fill the gap.

Fluke are the softer story this week, and it's worth being straight about it — the warm surface layer has spread fish out across the flats rather than concentrating them, and catch rates on the open bottom have thinned out accordingly. The better numbers are still coming from the deeper cuts, particularly the channel edges inside Plum Gut and the deeper holes along the Sluiceway between Little Gull and Great Gull Island, where a cooler bottom layer persists even with the surface running warm. Four-inch white Gulp on three-quarter-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom on the last of the outgoing, has been the more dependable combination there. Sea bass are holding as a steady secondary catch on the same structure — small jigs tipped with squid strips working the rockier stretches around Race Rock in twenty-five to forty feet.

Now for the one everybody's been asking about at the dock. Bonito are not here yet, but the signal is building fast. Block Island and Point Judith have the first confirmed fish of the season, and that bait behavior — squid and small baitfish tightening up along beaches and rip lines — is exactly the pattern that tends to walk west. We flagged this trend last week, saying it would push toward eastern Long Island Sound and the Race corridor within one to two weeks as water temperatures peak and start easing off, and that timeline still lines up. Anyone rigging ahead of the run should have half-ounce epoxy jigs in bone and green mackerel pattern ready for the Gut, along with small metal for when the fish are up on top working bait balls in the rip.

Looking at the next few days, expect the pattern to hold rather than shift hard. The moon is building toward full, which means stronger tidal swings and sharper, shorter slack windows through the Race and the Gut — good news for anyone who can time the last hour of the ebb precisely, tougher for anyone fishing loose on the clock. If the overnight air keeps trending cooler into the weekend, look for the first hints of the eastern Sound's surface temperature easing down a notch, which should extend the daytime striper window slightly and could be the trigger that finally pulls the first bonito west into Fishers Island Sound. Until then, the safe bet remains wire line and bucktails on the Race Rock-to-Valiant stretch on the last two hours of the ebb, with a backup drift into the Gut's deeper cuts for fluke and sea bass when the current lays down.
